title: Buildings With an Ocean View
statement:
A row of `n` buildings stands along a coast. The ocean lies to the **right** of the last building (beyond index `n - 1`). You are given the building heights `heights[0..n-1]`, listed from left to right.

A building has an **ocean view** if every building to its right is **strictly shorter** than it. A building with the same height as it, or taller, blocks the view. The last building always has a view because nothing stands to its right.

Print the indices (0-indexed) of all buildings with an ocean view, in **increasing** order.

**Follow-up:** (1) Suppose there is ocean on **both** sides, left and right. Return the buildings that see the ocean on at least one side. (2) You are now allowed to remove exactly one building. Which building should you remove to maximise the number of buildings that have a view? Think about what changes when a building disappears: only buildings whose view was blocked by it alone can gain a view.
inputFormat:
The first line contains an integer `n`.
The second line contains `n` integers: `heights[0], ..., heights[n-1]`.
outputFormat: Print the indices of buildings with an ocean view, space-separated, in increasing order.

examples.explanation: Building 3 (height 1) sees the ocean. Building 2 (height 3) is taller than everything to its right, so it sees too. Building 1 (height 2) is blocked by building 2. Building 0 (height 4) is taller than 2, 3 and 1, so it sees. Answer: `0 2 3`.

Building 4 always has a view. Building 3 has height 4, equal to its right neighbour, so it is blocked (the view requires strictly shorter buildings). Buildings 0 to 2 all have the 4s to their right, which are taller, so they are blocked too. Only building 4 has a view.
Heights strictly decrease, so every building looks over everything to its right: `0 1 2 3`.

hints: Checking each building against all buildings to its right works but is O(n^2). What single piece of information about the right side do you actually need?
A building has a view exactly when it is taller than the maximum height to its right. Walk from the right end towards the left while remembering the tallest height seen so far.
Collect indices as you walk right to left, then reverse the list so the output is increasing. Use strict comparison: an equal height blocks the view.
